title: What comes out (Mark 7:14–23)
hook: it's not what goes in that defiles, but what comes out of the heart

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was tradition, what's handed on, and a holy word used as a loophole. Your line was keep the heart of it. Which habit did you check? Day one hundred eighty-seven.

A whole day of careful eating: vegetables, water, vitamins. And then someone cuts in on the highway, or a coworker takes credit for the work, and what comes out is something nobody's grandmother should hear. Everything that went in was careful. What came out wasn't. After the argument about washed hands, Jesus calls the whole crowd back to him and says, listen, all of you, and understand. Then he says something so short it sounds like a riddle. Today: what comes out.
screen: `CAREFUL ABOUT WHAT GOES IN.` → `THEN SOMEONE CUTS YOU OFF.` → `LISTEN, ALL OF YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the riddle, in the old King James Bible: "There is nothing from without a man, that entering into him can defile him: but the things which come out of him, those are they that defile the man." Defile, in Greek, is a word that means to make common, to make something ordinary that was meant to be set apart. Later, indoors, the disciples ask him about it, and he's a bit exasperated again: "Are ye so without understanding also?" Food goes into the stomach, he says, not into the heart, and then out again. But "from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts," and he names a long list: thefts, murders, greed, deceit, envy, pride, foolishness. That's what really makes a person unclean. Mark adds a short note of his own here; the King James words it purging all meats, and some Christian readers take it as Jesus declaring all foods clean. Some Christians point to it when asked why they don't keep the food laws of the Torah. Jews who keep kosher understand those laws as God's commandments to Israel, and keep them with devotion; and scholars differ on how much Mark's note meant at the time. Either way, the center of the teaching is the heart. In the Bible, the heart isn't only feelings. It's where you think, decide and choose. It's the kitchen where words get cooked before they're served. So Jesus moves the question from the plate to the source. Not only, what did I take in today? But, what came out?
screen: `NOTHING FROM WITHOUT CAN DEFILE.` · `DEFILE — TO MAKE COMMON.` · `OUT OF THE HEART PROCEED.` · `THE HEART: WHERE YOU CHOOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch what comes out of your mouth. Settle, and breathe. Replay the last day. Not what you ate or watched. What you said. The kind words. The sharp ones. The joke at someone's expense. The complaint you repeated. Don't punish yourself. Just notice where each one came from: tired, scared, jealous, generous, glad. If you pray, you can ask God for a clean heart. If not, just choose one word you'd like to say more of today. The bell holds the time.
Defile, what Jesus said doesn't come from the plate but from the heart: evil thoughts, not food, are what truly defile a person.
Your line: from the heart. Today, before one sharp word leaves your mouth, pause, and ask where it's coming from. Day one hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Christians do not, as a rule, keep the Torah's food laws, and some point to this passage when asked why; some also practice an examination of conscience at the end of the day, looking back over what they said and did.

original.note: Greek: to make common, to defile, from koinos, common, shared.

trapdoor: what you thought: a teaching about food.
what it means: Jesus moves the question from the plate to the heart: what comes out of you shows what's inside.
what a scholar hears: koinoo, to make common. Mark's aside on food is read by some as declaring all foods clean, and debated by scholars.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: the vice list included 'cruelty', which is not in Mark 7:21–22; now thefts, murders, greed, deceit, envy, pride, foolishness. Hook rewritten (it opened 'You've probably had this day' and told the listener what they'd said); cut 'most churches', 'almost everyone agrees' and 'many Christians' claims.

Mark 7:19b (Greek katharizōn panta ta brōmata; KJV 'purging all meats') is widely read as 'thus he declared all foods clean'; the script attributes this reading to 'many Christians' and notes scholarly debate. Judaism and Christianity Keepers should confirm the kosher sentence is fair and non-ranking.
